summary: Describes a flexible way to represent time values, such as an interval or a duration, in the generalized MANET packet and message format. It defines Message and Address Block TLVs for validity and interval times.

eli5.summary: Wireless networks of moving devices need to say how long information stays fresh. This note defines a standard little label that carries those time amounts in their messages.

questions: how are validity times represented in manet
what is the multi-value time tlv
what is a time tlv in manet
how is time encoded in 8 bits
subtitle: A compact 8-bit way for MANET routers to say how long information stays valid or how often it will be refreshed.

tldr.problem: MANET routing protocols need to state intervals and validity durations, from sub-second to many days, in very few bits because wireless bandwidth is limited.
tldr.mechanism: A time is stored in one 8-bit time-code (3 mantissa bits, 5 exponent bits) scaled by a constant C. A Time TLV can carry several time-codes tied to hop-count ranges. Two TLVs, INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME, are defined for messages and address blocks.
tldr.outcome: Routing protocols built on the RFC 5444 packet format can share one time encoding instead of each inventing their own. The RFC defines a format, not a protocol.

today: RFC 5497 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Why Time Needs Its Own TLV
sections.content:
The generalized packet and message format of RFC 5444 lets Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) routing protocols attach attributes to packets, messages or addresses using a TLV (type-length-value structure). This RFC defines a general Time TLV for expressing a single time-value, or a set of time-values each tied to a range of hop counts.

A time-value here is not a point on the clock. It is an interval or a duration, such as 10 seconds. The RFC defines two uses: INTERVAL_TIME, the maximum time before another message of the same type from the same originator should arrive, and VALIDITY_TIME, how long the information stays valid after receipt. When both are present the validity time is usually the larger, to allow for lost messages.
sections.eli5: When you tell a friend some news, you can also say how often you will update them and how long the news stays true. This note gives routers a short way to say both things.

sections.title: Motivation: Wide Range, Few Bits
sections.content:
Different MANET protocols and deployments want different timing. A fast-changing network may want sub-second message spacing, while a stable one may want multi-hour spacing. At the same time, MANETs use bandwidth-limited wireless interfaces, so protocols prefer to spend a little computation to save bits. Interval and validity times do not need high precision, which makes this trade-off practical.

The design therefore encodes a time in an 8-bit field, lets values range from very small (for example 1/1024 second) to very long (for example 45 days), and lets a protocol or deployment tune this through one parameter, C. The parameter C must be the same for all MANET routers in the same deployment.
sections.eli5: Wireless gadgets have very little room for messages, so every bit counts. One small number can stand for anything from a blink to weeks, a bit like a stopwatch that counts in bigger and bigger steps.

sections.title: How a Time Is Encoded
sections.content:
Each time-value is stored as an 8-bit time-code. The least significant 3 bits are the mantissa a and the most significant 5 bits are the exponent b:

  • time-value := (1 + a/8) * 2^b * C
  • time-code := 8 * b + a

All nodes in the MANET MUST use the same value of the constant C, in seconds, and C MUST be greater than 0. Larger time-codes always mean larger time-values, so time-values can be compared by comparing time-codes. A protocol using this encoding MUST define C.

The smallest representable time-value is C. The largest is 15 * 2^28 * C, or about 4.0 * 10^9 * C; with C = 1/1024 second this is about 45 days. The RFC gives an algorithm for finding the smallest time-code whose time-value is not less than a wanted time t, which reports that the time cannot be represented when the exponent or mantissa falls out of range. A protocol MAY say that time-code 0 means a time of zero and/or that 255 means an indefinitely large time.
sections.eli5: Think of a ruler where the marks get farther apart as you go along. Small numbers are measured finely and big numbers roughly, so one byte can cover very short and very long times.

sections.title: The Time TLV Structure
sections.content:
The value of a Time TLV holds time-data: (<time-code><hop-count>)*<time-code>. That is zero or more pairs of a time-code and a hop count, followed by one default time-code. With n pairs it has 2n+1 octets, and the receiver finds n from the TLV length.

The hop counts MUST be strictly increasing and the last one less than 255. A receiver at a given hop count from the originator uses the first time-code whose hop count is greater than or equal to its own, and uses the default time-code if its hop count is larger than all of them. This suits messages sent with different hop limits, where far-away nodes see updates less often. If the message has no hop-count field, or the TLV is a Packet TLV, the hop count is defined as 255 and the single-code form (n = 0) SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: It is like a sign that says: if you live within 2 streets, expect mail every day; if farther, every week; and everyone else, every month. The router checks how far away it is and picks the right line.

sections.title: Single-Value and Multi-Value TLVs
sections.content:
A single-value Time TLV has the tismultivalue flag cleared and holds one time-data structure. It may be a Packet TLV, Message TLV or Address Block TLV. Its length MUST be 2n+1.

A multi-value Time TLV has tismultivalue set and holds one time-data structure per address in the address block, so each address can have its own time. It MUST be an Address Block TLV, never a Packet or Message TLV. Its length MUST be m * (2n+1), where m is number-values from RFC 5444. Every time-data structure MUST have the same number of pairs, although the hop-count lists MAY differ.
sections.eli5: A single-value TLV is one label for a whole parcel. A multi-value TLV is a sticker on each item in the parcel, so every item can have its own date.

sections.title: INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME
sections.content:
Both TLVs exist as Message TLVs and as Address Block TLVs, and a message MUST NOT include more than one of each Message TLV.

  • INTERVAL_TIME gives the maximum time before another message of the same type from the same originator should be received (for the Address Block form, one that contains this address). It MAY depend on hop count.
  • VALIDITY_TIME gives how long after receipt the content, or the addresses, count as valid. After that the receiver MUST treat them as no longer valid unless they are repeated in a later message.

If a protocol uses an Address Block TLV together with the Message TLV of the same name, it MUST say how to interpret both being present. The RFC suggests the address-level TLV overrides the message-level one for the addresses it covers.
sections.eli5: One label says how often to expect the next update. The other says how long the news can be trusted. If nothing new arrives before the time is up, throw the old news away.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated the same numbers to the Message TLV and Address Block TLV of the same name: INTERVAL_TIME is type 0 with type extension 0, and VALIDITY_TIME is type 1 with type extension 0. Other type extensions 1 to 223 are Expert Review and 224 to 255 are for Experimental Use. The RFC says the assignments were requested here to avoid interdependencies between unrelated MANET protocols and to avoid using up TLV type space on identical structures.
sections.eli5: The two labels got official numbers, like library catalogue numbers, so every MANET protocol that uses them means the same thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The threats are those of RFC 5444: loss of integrity and confidentiality. Changing a Time TLV can give information a wrong validity time or expected interval, causing incorrect protocol behavior. Adding timed information can raise workload, especially with short validity times, and storage needs, especially with long ones. The RFC points to the authentication and encryption suggestions in RFC 5444 as the countermeasure.
sections.eli5: If a bad actor changes the date stamp, routers might trust old news or ignore fresh news. Locking the message so nobody can change it helps.
